Norway's ice hockey team claims Russia replacing it at World Juniors

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (860 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With just weeks to go until the start of the 2027 World Junior Championship, it remains unclear who will be the 10th, and final, participant.
  • Recent findings suggest that the move, which has yet to be publicly announced by the IIHF, comes in apparent response to the Court of Arbitration (CAS) ruling in late October, which ordered it to allow Russia to return to international play.
  • The IIHF barred Russia and Belarus from international play shortly after Moscow released its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With just weeks to go until the start of the 2027 World Junior Championship, it remains unclear who will be the 10th, and final, participant. This comes after the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association noted the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) had said it had been removed from the tournament so that Russia could take part.

Recent findings suggest that the move, which has yet to be publicly announced by the IIHF, comes in apparent response to the Court of Arbitration (CAS) ruling in late October, which ordered it to allow Russia to return to international play. The World Juniors is the first tournament affected by the CAS decision.

The IIHF barred Russia and Belarus from international play shortly after Moscow released its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

In a statement issued Saturday, the IIHF mentioned it was "taking the necessary steps required by the CAS ruling and reviewing what conditions would need to be met to safeguard our Championships, protect the organization's financial stability and secure the long-term future of international ice hockey.".

Sources indicate that as of Monday, the IIHF website still listed Norway as one of the participants in the World Juniors, which is to be hosted by Edmonton and Red Deer, Alberta, beginning on December 26. But Swiss Ice Hockey has responded to Norway's statement, saying its team would not face Russia at the World Juniors — as would be the case if it replaces Norway in the schedule.

However, it's far from certain that Russia will actually be able to ice a team in the tournament, as just last week, the Canadian prime minister ruled out the possibility.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," mentioned Mark Carney.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there.".

How this circle could be squared is unclear. Carney's pledge, coupled with the stated refusal by Finland, Sweden, Switzerland and others to face Russia in an international tournament, appears to have given the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association (NIHF) hope that its team could still play in the upcoming tournament. Several long-time corporate sponsors have also threatened to pull out if Russia is allowed to compete.

"This makes us hope that the last word has not been said about our participation in Canada in December," said NIHF General Secretary Petter Salsten.

"The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association is awaiting further information from the IIHF in the coming days.".

Meanwhile, the German Ice Hockey Association (DEB) is still in discussions with the government in Berlin and the IIHF about how to proceed — or not — with hosting the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship in May.

"We intend to host the world championship in Germany next year, and I am very optimistic that we will succeed in doing so," DEB chairman Frank H. Lutz told German broadcaster MagentaSport on Saturday.

While he acknowledged the IIHF's CAS-ordered requirement to include Russia and reiterated the DEB's rejection of the court ruling, he provided no indication as to how this obstacle could be overcome.

Lutz, who mentioned he would be in Berlin for more consultations this week, had previously said handing back Germany's hosting rights was a possibility — if only as a last resort.

On Friday, government spokesman Stefan Kornelius mentioned Berlin supports the DEB's efforts to find a solution.

It has been revealed that "However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore, through dialogue, how we can still ensure the tournament takes place.".

Asked at the same press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman indicated that this would be difficult under restrictions currently in place.

"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," said spokesperson Martin Giese.

However, he did not categorically rule out the possibility.

It has been suggested that government officials could be choosing their words carefully out of concern for Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees who are bidding to host an Olympic Games — like the German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) — to follow its lead.

Asked whether the debate over Russia's possible involvement in a hockey tournament could affect Munich's chances, government spokesman Kornelius stated he didn't wish to "speculate on implications.".

Still, with the IOC set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process, one has to think that the glitch could hardly have come up at a more inopportune time for the DOSB.

Roberto De Zerbi eager to sign Nottingham Forest star for Tottenham

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tottenham manager Roberto De Zerbi is reportedly very keen on a potential transfer deal for Nottingham Forest striker Liam Delap.
  • The north London giants could do with strengthening up front as soon as possible, and it seems that Delap is someone they’re strongly interested in for that position.
  • Still, a January deal is seen as difficult, with De Zerbi seemingly prepared to wait until next summer to try to bring Delap to Spurs, according to Football Transfers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tottenham manager Roberto De Zerbi is reportedly very keen on a potential transfer deal for Nottingham Forest striker Liam Delap.

The north London giants could do with strengthening up front as soon as possible, and it seems that Delap is someone they’re strongly interested in for that position.

Still, a January deal is seen as difficult, with De Zerbi seemingly prepared to wait until next summer to try to bring Delap to Spurs, according to Football Transfers.

The 23-year-old has started well at Forest after a difficult spell at Chelsea, scoring three goals in nine Premier League games so far this season after managing just one in 28 appearances at Stamford Bridge.

Our understanding is that Tottenham may also have other striker targets alongside Delap, as we recently reported here via the Daily Briefing.

De Zerbi inherited a struggling Spurs squad when he took over late on last season and narrowly helped the team avoid relegation from the Premier League.

There was significant investment in the summer as Sandro Tonali and Mateus Fernandes came in in midfield, but someone like Delap could be a useful addition to help continue to take this project forwards.

It’s not been an easy position for Tottenham in recent times, as Mathys Tel has mostly struggled since joining, while Randal Kolo Muani’s loan move last season proved unsuccessful.

Delap ticks a lot of boxes as he’s young and has the potential to keep improving whilst also already showing what he can do in the Premier League with his fine form for Forest and for former club Ipswich Town.

'If you don't give him what he wants, he'll burn your house down': Inside the 'cult' of Sir Jim Ratcliffe, as sources from his crumbling sporting empire reveal the destructive know-it-all arrogance of Man United co-owner and his henchmen

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1621 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 12:00 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 12:11 EST, 19 November 2026.
  • Sources indicate that the flat rural acres of the Turweston Aerodrome, in the north-west corner of Buckinghamshire, are far enough from human habitation for anyone padlocked in a building out there to feel seriously threatened.
  • The ‘imprisonment’ of the four-time British Olympic champion in a building, with signs declaring ‘No Entry’ fixed to the external doors, was one of the more extraordinary allegations to emerge from the court case, settled this week, over a £180million yacht Ratcliffe and Ainslie built together for the 2024 America’s Cup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 12:00 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 12:11 EST, 19 November 2026.

Sources indicate that the flat rural acres of the Turweston Aerodrome, in the north-west corner of Buckinghamshire, are far enough from human habitation for anyone padlocked in a building out there to feel seriously threatened. And if the testimony of Sir Ben Ainslie is to be believed, that’s what can come of crossing swords with Sir Jim Ratcliffe and Ineos.

The ‘imprisonment’ of the four-time British Olympic champion in a building, with signs declaring ‘No Entry’ fixed to the external doors, was one of the more extraordinary allegations to emerge from the court case, settled this week, over a £180million yacht Ratcliffe and Ainslie built together for the 2024 America’s Cup.

Ratcliffe, who had withdrawn financial support, was demanding the team’s assets and intellectual property, and, according to court papers, Ineos representative Raymond Fellows, assisted by two security contractors, arrived at the offices of Ainslie's Athena Racing and applied his own chain and padlock. He’d been refused the keys by the building’s owner. Ainslie and his financial officer Matt Robinson managed to leave the building through the fire escape.

Ineos were applying petrochemicals business methods to sport, as usual. Fellows had also been employed by Ratcliffe to provide security assistance amid protests at Ineos’ controversial British fracking sites. The experienced security industry executive observed that ‘a small hard core group of activists’ was at work and that social media surveillance was useful, according to court papers from an earlier case.

Ineos denied the ‘false imprisonment’ of Ainslie, insisting that their employee had padlocked the building to prevent anyone entering, not knowing that someone was inside and that, in any case, there were ‘alternative exit routes’.

But the organization did not entirely challenge Ainslie’s claim that Rob Nevin, chairman of Ratcliffe’s sports division and a Manchester United board member, had told him during a heated meeting about the disputed boat in Barcelona: ‘We have a phrase at Ineos: scorched earth. It means that if you don’t give Jim what he wants, he will burn your house down, or words to that effect.’.

Sir Jim Ratcliffe's relationship with his one-time friend Ben Ainslie ruptured after Ineos withdrew support for the latter's America’s Cup bid.

Ratcliffe's running of Manchester United is criticised by one anonymous source. ‘People like him see football on TV and just assume they can do it,’ they say.

That threat, which Ineos say was only made figuratively, illustrates how Ratcliffe runs his businesses with what several sources describe as a cult-like authority, full of such maxims and mantras laid down to staff who fear him.

That ‘cult of Sir Jim’ is born of the billionaire’s own immense air of superiority and is something he seems to have instilled in some of his most senior executives.

Recent findings suggest that nevin, 68, a long-standing Ratcliffe lieutenant, has informed some who have encountered him since he arrived at Old Trafford that he has completed 60 or more major ‘transactions’ – business deals – in the oil and gas industry. He is described as ‘not short on confidence’.

Recent findings suggest that nevin chairs Ineos Sport, the collection of acquisitions built up when Ratcliffe believed his firm could straddle multiple sports and succeed at all of them, in the style of Red Bull. Ratcliffe disastrously installed his brother, Bob, as chief executive at OGC Nice, the second of the football teams he bought, and that air of superiority and ‘always knowing’ has been manifest at United, too.

Recent findings suggest that ratcliffe demonstrated to some of the Manchester United players the stretches he was using for London Marathon training, after buying the club. He considered his friend Sir Dave Brailsford to be ‘best in class’ when it came to running the football side of the club, despite the former Team Sky cycling chief only having a loose connection of football contacts, mostly picked up from his appearances on the Leaders in Sport conference circuit for his friend Jimmy Worrall, the entrepreneur who set up that business.

Sources have told us that Brailsford was so enamoured with Manchester City, after arriving to ‘save United’, that he and other Ineos people were ‘skipping around’ when Omar Berrada, chief operations officer at the Etihad, was hired as chief executive.

‘There was no sense from Ratcliffe of needing people who understand the industry and its craft,’ claims one source, speaking on condition of anonymity. ‘People like this see football on TV and just assume they can do it.’.

Ratcliffe (pictured next to former United boss Erik ten Hag) inexplicably considered Dave Brailsford (right) to be ‘best in class’ when it came to running the football side of the club.

Rob Nevin (right) chairs Ineos Sport, the collection of acquisitions built up when Ratcliffe wrongly believed his firm could straddle multiple sports and succeed at all of them.

None of Ratcliffe’s executives will be wanting to tell him that. A further sense of what a formidable presence he is for his own staff came in a 30-minute ‘Ask Jim’ interview with him, conducted by his own director of corporate affairs, Tom Crotty, this summer.

Ratcliffe stares at the floor for much of the time as Crotty bowls him a series of long-hop questions and he seems profoundly miserable, revealing little more than his unhappiness with the British government’s management of North Sea oilfields and his dislike for the British sports press.

The interview was conducted the day after the World Cup final between Spain and Argentina in July, which Ratcliffe attended. ‘It was fabulous. A great celebration, despite the whining British press who really didn’t like it,’ he says.

It has been revealed that asked how he switches off, he cites time on the golf driving range and fishing on his salmon farm in Iceland – to which Berrada and the Glazers have had to make their way for some executive meetings. ‘Biggest lessons learned in 2025?’ There don’t appear to have been any. At no stage do United feature.

Ratcliffe trots out his extremely well-worn mantra about the major three traits Ineos prize most – ‘Grit, rigour, humour’ – informing the relentlessly positive Crotty of the need to ‘do work properly before you make important decisions, because you need to spend capital well.’.

In a recent development, that’s not happened in sport. The extraordinary rupture with Ainslie, after Ineos withdrew support for a third America’s Cup cycle and he continued to use the boat, is part of a general, hugely acrimonious winding down of the Ineos Sport masterplan.

OGC Nice and FC Lausanne-Sport, Ratcliffe’s European football clubs, are up for sale amid fan protest, while it is widely expected that Ineos will eventually disappear from cycling. They have already diluted their involvement, with the team formerly known as the Ineos Grenadiers now co-sponsored by Danish technology firm Netcompany. The All Blacks and Tottenham Hotspur both sued Ineos for prematurely terminating commercial relationships. Both parties ultimately reached a confidential legal settlement with the tech giant.

What United need, as they look to Mauricio Pochettino for deliverance, is for Ratcliffe to climb down from his lofty peak, display some of the humility which has been missing and admit there have been faults.

What United need, as they look to Mauricio Pochettino for deliverance, is for Ratcliffe to display some humility.

The club's executives, including CEO Omar Berrada (centre) and director of football Jason Wilcox (right), have appeared out of their depth and in need of support.

Industry observers note that the view among some outsiders who interact at a high level with the club is, in the words of one, that United are ‘the biggest club in the world and yet no longer the biggest club in the world'. They carry huge expectation, yet are unable to compete for transfer fees and wages with Barcelona, Real Madrid, Bayern Munich, Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester City, and have removed excellent staff without replacing them. To cite only one, Victoria Timpson secured the club’s lucrative Snapdragon sponsorship deal but still departed.

Sources indicate that ‘If United were an iPhone, someone would need to unfold the paper clip pretty quick, push it in the side of the phone and hard restart everything,’ states the aforementioned source. 'The club need a genuinely industry-leading chief executive, a sporting director of the calibre of Edwin van der Sar who, unlike Jason Wilcox, has the experience, pedigree and knowledge he accumulated as CEO at Ajax. They need a boardroom presence and link to the fans like Bryan Robson.'.

Ratcliffe does not even sit on the United board himself, leaving it to Nevin and John Reece, one of the Ineos co-founders.

According to recent reports, another of his Ineos appointees was the 63-year-old Frenchman Jean-Claude Blanc, an experienced statesman and marketeer with an Olympic, Tour de France and PSG background, who is described as pleasant and without ego – though he was supposedly in the room when the 'scorched' earth comment was made to Ainslie. Blanc was recruited for his gravitas, rather than to pull up trees. He has stepped down from United's board.

Ainslie and Ratcliffe are no longer thought to be friends. Shortly before the alleged episode in the locked aerodrome building, Ainslie observed, in relation to Ratcliffe, that there was a difference between business and sport, where teams were delicately balanced, nuanced groups of people.

Sources indicate that ‘You want to save money and be efficient, but you’ve got to make sure you look after people. You need that balance,’ he stated. Under the terms of the court settlement, Ainslie gets to keep the boat and sail off into the sunset, leaving Ratcliffe to whatever storms come next.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tottenham will be looking to get back to winning ways when they return to Premier League action against Ipswich Town on Saturday afternoon.

After moving out of the relegation zone with three wins from three in October, the Lilywhites crashed back down to earth with a slender 1-0 defeat at Leeds United just prior to November's international break.

The home encounter against Ipswich represents a chance to claim another three points for Roberto De Zerbi's men, although the match will be far from straightforward as the Tractor Boys have made a decent start to life back in the Premier League with three wins from their first ten league games under Gary O'Neil.

De Zerbi has some substantial calls to make in regards to his team, with Mathys Tel set to miss a period of action after suffering an injury at Leeds following a challenge by Jayden Bogle.

One player who could potentially make his return to the team is Savio following a month on the sidelines due to a muscle injury sustained in the draw at Manchester United.

The Brazilian winger started on the left at Old Trafford and he may quite well come straight into the team if fit and take Tel's place on the left flank for the home encounter against Ipswich.

De Zerbi may also have Mykhailo Mudryk at his disposal again following an ankle injury sustained in training.

The loan signing's only appearance in a Tottenham shirt came at the start of September with a 16-minute cameo off the bench against Nottingham Forest.

Mudryk will be desperate to make up for lost time and show everyone exactly why he was brought to Tottenham on loan in the first place.

Mudryk and Savio's 2026/27 season in numbers.

Tottenham supporters are desperate to see more of Savio in the starting XI with injury restricting him to only six appearances following his substantial-money move from Man City.

The 22-year-old, who was labelled as "incredible" by Pep Guardiola during his time at Man City, had a Spurs debut to remember after registering one goal and one assist against Charlton Athletic in the Carabao Cup in August, thus seeing Roberto De Zerbi label it as the "perfect day" for his fresh signing.

Savio fared well in his last appearance in the draw at Manchester United, delivering a bright performance but unfortunately it was his end product that let him down at times.

It should be a rather straightforward call for De Zerbi to make between Savio and Mudryk, with the ex-City winger ahead of his competitor when it comes to starting for Tottenham.

If indeed Savio does feature against Ipswich, it is a huge opportunity for him to try and cement his place in De Zerbi's side with some winnable games coming up prior to next month's North London Derby.

#2044. Industry News: Aberdeen's newly introduced manager is a proven overachiever with a substantial personality... but can Dons get a bounce from their Super Mario?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1349 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dailymail ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Aberdeen's newly introduced manager is a proven overachiever with a substantial personality... but can Dons get a bounce from their Super Mario?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1349 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.
  • Published: 15:12 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 15:20 EST, 19 November 2026.
  • Stephen Robinson was probably destined to fail at Aberdeen in any event.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.

Published: 15:12 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 15:20 EST, 19 November 2026.

Stephen Robinson was probably destined to fail at Aberdeen in any event. While unquestionably a successful manager with Motherwell and St Mirren, there was always a lingering doubt about whether his skill set would work at a bigger club with different expectations in terms of style of play. And so it proved.

What didn’t help the Northern Irishman was the perception that those who employed him weren’t exactly bowled over by him in the first place, either.

Robinson would have been a hard enough sell to the Dons support had he been unveiled a few days after Jimmy Thelin departed the scene in January.

That it took them 67 days to deliver confirmation of the appointment – after the club had dalliances with Eirik Horneland and Sandro Schwarz – was hardly a ringing endorsement of their faith in him.

The contrast with the process to appoint Mario Frick is striking. Robinson was sacked two days after a four-goal home thrashing by Hibernian. Five days later, the former Liechtenstein international was named by the Pittodrie club as the upcoming head coach.

After the saga at the start of the year which reflected well on no one, Aberdeen, to give them their dues, knew what they wanted and saw Frick as a hand-in-glove fit. So, what led them so promptly to his door?

Mario Frick is unveiled at Pittodrie and immediately vowed to transform the club's fortunes.

The 52-year-old, essentially, is a head coach who fits in with the overarching strategy Aberdeen identified several years ago.

This has been lost along the way as poor results have seen a churn of individuals occupy the dug-out, many of whom were square pegs in round holes. This, the club believe, has been why the recruitment has been so random and ineffective.

There’s been little joined-up thinking, as evidenced by the summer window which saw 15 players arrive, many of whom were sub-standard or clearly not part of Robinson’s blueprint.

The intention always was for the head coach to work in tandem with the sporting director and chief executive rather than independently of them.

While Frick will have a say on what players arrive and depart this January, the conversations around the identity of the team and what’s required to improve it will be three-way.

At Luzern, Frick was happy to trust the judgment of director of football Remo Meyer on such matters.

His willingness to forge the same relationship with Aberdeen’s sporting director, Lutz Pfannenstiel, was the light bulb moment for chief executive Adrian Bevington and chairman Dave Cormack.

Frick earned 125 caps for Liechtenstein and scored 16 goals for the European minnows.

It has been revealed that in keeping with the much-vaunted ‘continental’ model, Pfannenstiel and head of recruitment Darren Mowbray will largely identify players to fit the system. Frick will then be tasked with making it all work.

The plan is for the squad to be closely aligned with the head coach’s needs rather than assembling the rag bag of players who’ve come in the three windows since Thelin won the Scottish Cup.

There’s much beyond Frick’s willingness to defer matters of player identification to others which caught the eye of the board, however.

Although very much a modern and forward-thinking coach, he’s vastly experienced in the game.

As a player, he turned out for Swiss clubs including St Gallen, Basel, Zurich and Grasshopper.

He became the first Liechtensteiner to play professionally in Italy with AC Arezzo before signing for Verona, Ternana and Siena.

Across 125 internationals, he became Liechtenstein’s all-time top scorer with 16 goals, including one against Scotland at Hampden in 2010, the infamous game which saw Stephen McManus ride to the rescue with a 90th-minute winner.

Aberdeen chief executive Adrian Bevington welcomes upcoming manager Frick to Pittodrie.

Being the star man for an underdog may have had something to do with his upbringing. Frick’s father didn’t exactly encourage him to make it as he started out in the game.

Recent findings suggest that he once revealed in an interview: ‘He told me: ‘There are thousands of talents like you. You won’t make it.’.

His coaching journey began eight years ago with Vaduz, who he succeeded in getting promoted to the Swiss Super League via a play-off.

Industry observers note that appointed head coach of Luzern almost five years ago, he turned the side from relegation candidates into one capable of finishing fourth inside 18 months. There followed finishes of seventh, sixth and seventh place prior to an amicable parting of the ways when his contract expired in May.

Although Frick didn’t win anything, Luzern is not a club which is accustomed to doing so, with their last league title arriving in 1989.

Its supporters still strongly identified with him, though, and recognised that he often got more out of modest resources than he was entitled to.

They enjoyed his big personality – not scared to wind up opponents in the media and not shy at publicly calling out his own players when they didn’t live up to the standards he’d set.

Frick famously scored for Liechtenstein against Scotland in a 2-1 at Hampden in 2010.

When he left there at the end of last season, the supporters felt the loss of a passionate manager who wore his heart on his sleeve, had no time for egos and stopped at nothing to deliver success.

In the Granite City, he will call out anyone not giving their absolute all every moment they are in a red jersey. And unlike the diplomatic Thelin, the fireworks are likely to be seen in public.

Industry observers note that if his time at Luzern proves prescient, those who resist or disrupt the dressing room will soon be moved on. Those who do their best by him will have nothing to fear, however.

As Italian football fan Fabio Baccarini will gladly attest, although tough and demanding, Frick is also renowned as being a loyal man with a huge heart.

Baccarini, from Reggio Emilia, became fascinated by Frick in the early 2000s while collecting Panini stickers due to the fact that he played for Liechtenstein, a tiny nation he struggled to pronounce.

He wrote so many letters to his various clubs, hoping to arrange a meeting, that Frick initially feared he might be a stalker.

When they first met in 2011 after a game between Liechtenstein and San Marino, the forward presented Baccarini with a signed shirt, gave him his email address and invited him to a match in Vaduz.

And so began an extraordinary friendship which saw Baccarini regularly drive 1,000km to support the minnows and become their de facto mascot.

In a recent development, three years back, when Hibs travelled to Luzern in the Conference League, the Italian super-fan was unable to find a bed for the night. Frick ensured he got one in the team hotel at no cost.

The upcoming Pittodrie boss is just the latest to follow in the footsteps of the great Sir Alex Ferguson.

As heartwarming as such tales are, it was, of course, the metrics of on-field success which drew Aberdeen to him.

Frick’s willingness to give young players a chance – another criticism made of Robinson – was a tick against his name.

It has been revealed that he’s handed top-flight debuts to more than 30 academy players during his coaching career. He appointed Ardon Jashari, who played against Scotland on Monday, his Luzern captain at the age of 20.

According to recent reports, he does not appear to be wedded to a particular formation. He mostly played a 4-4-2 with a diamond at Luzern, but he’s very much a pragmatist.

When he takes his bow at Rugby Park on Saturday, he’ll select a system to suit the personnel rather than trying to shoehorn the players into a pre-ordained system.

With just two points separating their team from bottom-side Kilmarnock, how the Red Army could do with witnessing a Super Mario bounce.

Pep Guardiola has emerged as the dream candidate after leaving Manchester City in the summer, while Nashville SC boss BJ Callaghan and USMNT Under-23s coach Steve Cherundolo are the current favourites.

When assessing Henry's credentials, he noted: "Yeah, I’d buy him too, just because of being around him, the way he sees the game, the confidence that he would give those players.

"I think when he’s telling them stuff, they’re going to listen.

According to recent reports, “There’s a reason why there’s a statue outside of the Arsenal stadium, the Emirates, of him, because of what he was able to do. He’s one of the best players to have played the game. So if he can figure out a way to give some of that confidence and that knowledge of the game to some of these players, I think it could make a significant difference.".

Dempsey has worked with the Arsenal and France icon on CBS Sports' coverage of the Champions League. He claimed Henry had previously told him that it's a job he would like.

He continued: "In the Olympics, he was able to get France to a second-place finish versus Spain. He’s someone who loves the game. He loves the US. He’s passionate about it. He loves New York, the time that he spent there. So, you know, I say, why not?

"Because someone of his pedigree, and being around the game, and me watching the way that he watches the game and sees football, I think there’s a lot of positives there. I know that it’s a job that he would want to do because we’ve had conversations about it. And I think he’s someone who could make a difference.".

Henry spent four years of his playing career in the US, representing the Upcoming York Red Bulls in a significant coup for the MLS. After ending his on-pitch career in the Significant Apple, he has regularly been seen on UK and US television as a popular pundit.

Industry observers note that however, he has also dipped his toes into coaching and management. Henry was appointed by AS Monaco in 2018, but lasted just 20 matches, in which he won five.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Global carbon emissions are set to slightly drop this year, a latest study suggests, largely as a result of high energy prices in the wake of the US war on Iran and the disruption of supply through the Strait of Hormuz.
  • Recent findings suggest that emissions from oil, gas and coal are the main drivers of climate change.
  • "It's downwards, which sounds good, but this is largely driven by the war in Iran, what's happened in the Strait of Hormuz," said the study's co-author Glen Peters, a scientist at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research in Norway.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Global carbon emissions are set to slightly drop this year, a latest study suggests, largely as a result of high energy prices in the wake of the US war on Iran and the disruption of supply through the Strait of Hormuz.

Recent findings suggest that emissions from oil, gas and coal are the main drivers of climate change. While over the past decade, these emissions have risen by 0.9% per year, they are expected to drop by 0.4% in 2026.

"It's downwards, which sounds good, but this is largely driven by the war in Iran, what's happened in the Strait of Hormuz," said the study's co-author Glen Peters, a scientist at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research in Norway.

"So in a way, a little bit of good news, but for the wrong reasons.".

The study was released while global leaders are meeting in Turkey for the United Nations' COP31 climate conference.

Sources indicate that the study published by international research group the Global Carbon Project found that oil emissions dropped by 1.9% in 2026, while natural gas fell by 0.3%. Coal emissions however continued to rise, by around 0.6%.

"A drop in emissions in ‌one year is not a peak unless it ‌is driven ​by structural change," Peters cautioned.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

A structural change would mean that emissions would slowly rise to a peak and then slowly decline afterward, indicating a long term trend. That's not what happened though, Peters mentioned. "What we see this year is [that] oil emissions are going up and then suddenly, bang, down 2%.".

In a recent development, it is the third time in recent years that global carbon pollution has dropped. The previous declines were during the global economic crisis in 2009 and during the COVID pandemic in 2020. In each of those cases, emissions went back up once global economies recovered.

While the geopolitical shocks of the past year have been the driving factors behind the temporary emissions reversal, there has also been a rise in renewable energy contributing to the data. So while solar panels, wind farms and electric vehicles did make a difference, they were just not enough to cut emissions by themselves.

"The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies," according to co-author of the study, Pierre Friedlingstein, of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University.

And even though emissions from fossil fuels dropped slightly, overall global carbon dioxide emissions still went up by about 1%, the study warns. The overall rise is because of land use changes like deforestation and peat fires, which increased too fast to be offset by the slight decrease in fossil fuel burning.

David Moyes took a glug of water and glanced up at the massive screen away to his right, almost as if he wanted confirmation that what he was seeing was true.

Had he looked behind him, Moyes would have seen Andy Burnham and his wife, Marie-France, in raptures, along with thousands of others. It was true, all right. Everton had scored their third goal and were bounding into the Carabao Cup quarter-finals, seemingly without a care in the world.

What a happy change of direction. Moyes has spent months spinning plates, dealing with owners who do not care about a proud club and want to sell up and a squad that was left criminally short in the transfer window. Then, before Newcastle’s visit, came more disruption.

Jack Grealish’s selfish and reckless decision to go Awol from training on Monday could have been a catalyst for more misery and invited Newcastle to deliver a hammer blow to Everton’s season, but again, Moyes fostered a siege mentality. He was rewarded in the most emphatic fashion.

True, Newcastle collapsed like a deckchair without hinges and this performance – which encouraged many of their 8,000 followers to head for the exits early – would not have done anything to convince those who view Matthias Jaissle, the head coach, with ambivalence to change their minds.

In a recent development, the lack of discipline in their ranks was exposed when Dan Burn scored a late consolation and ended up in a melee with James Tarkowski and Joelinton. But the issues Jaissle, who lamented that “we must improve”, has to correct are for another day: this contest belonged to Everton.

According to recent reports, thierno Barry had provided the finish that secured a trip to Fleetwood in December and what an opportunity it is for Moyes to make Everton semi-finalists in this competition for the first time since 2016. Whether Grealish will have a part to play in it remains to be seen.

Thierno Barry with Everton's third! 🔵 https://t.co/dyb8fKud8N.

According to recent reports, the last thing Everton needed on a night of such importance was a distraction. Grealish will have a tough job mending relations, particularly with Moyes, but there was a paradox: though he had caused a major problem for 90 minutes he became an irrelevance.

Moyes is impatient to give Evertonians a massive day out and his only focus was on crossing this hurdle – for all that Newcastle have had a turbulent start to the campaign, they are dangerous opponents and you wondered in the fraught opening 30 minutes if they might exacerbate the hosts’ woes.

As Jaissle hopped and squirmed on the sidelines, imploring Newcastle forward, chances came and went: Harvey Barnes had a header saved, Fabian Schar tested Jordan Pickford from 30 yards while Vitalii Mykolenko and James Tarkowski made huge goal-saving challenges.

According to recent reports, “We should have scored more goals,” Jaissle, who was dressed as if auditioning for the role of The Milk Tray Man, growled. “It [losing] was shocking as the game was not that bad.”.

Moyes was infuriated by Everton’s initial inertia, so much so there was a point when the Scot prevented Merlin Röhl, his own full-back, from taking a throw-in until Tarkowski and Jake O’Brien had complied with his gesturing to get 10 yards further forward.

According to recent reports, it might have looked old-fashioned but it worked. Suddenly Everton started asking questions, Hayden Hackney almost got on the end of a cross from Mykolenko, and it encouraged the supporters on the vertiginous South Stand to raise their voices and become more involved.

According to recent reports, what they needed was a goal to set things alight and in the 34th minute, it arrived. Tyrique George won possession by Newcastle’s corner flag, the ball dropped at Hackney’s feet and he instinctively ushered it on to James Garner, who whipped a right-footed drive beyond Lukáš Horníček.

Recent findings suggest that james Garner puts Everton in front against Newcastle in the Carabao Cup! 🔵 https://t.co/TzponbWyGU.

Industry observers note that the roar that greeted it was a mix of elation and wonder, relief and desperation. The locals have grown weary of seeing nights with potential end in disappointment but here was the foothold they craved and the opportunity they were ready to seize. Soon the lead would be doubled.

Hackney would score the goal, converting a super Barry cross, but let us acknowledge the fabulous refereeing of Farai Hallam, who waved play on when he might have whistled for a foul on Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall. And how Everton took advantage.

Hayden Hackney doubles Everton's advantage! 🔵 https://t.co/VIY0Iln3nI.

It must be said the officiating this week has, in the main, been outstanding. Watching a match without the persistent spectre of VAR has been liberating and you can see the referees have felt free to make decisions on instinct.

Recent findings suggest that the whole experience of knowing a contest cannot be re-refereed has been better for all. It will not catch on, sadly, because too many people have gone too far down the road with VAR, but we should embrace the purity of “old school football” while we can.

Evertonians – the Prime Minister included – certainly embraced the buffer of a second goal and the fact Hackney scored it also felt like a throwback: a player who was plucked out of the Championship in the summer and encouraged by Moyes to show he could make the next step up.

It has been revealed that he did that and so, too, did Everton, their progress was assured in the 69th minute when Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall dashed down the left and crossed for Barry to finish. Moyes puffed out his cheeks as it hit the net. He, more than most, deserved to enjoy this one.

England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland are co-hosting the tournament, but none of them will qualify automatically and will instead have to fight for their place at the home tournament. Northern Ireland are in the draw too, after losing their co-host status when Casement Park was dropped from the roster of potential venues.

Here's when the draw will take place, how it works, where to watch it in the UK and Ireland and the key dates for qualifying and the tournament itself.

After the announcement by the UK government in September 2024 that Northern Ireland's Casement Park would not receive funding to rebuild the stadium ahead of the tournament, the decision was made to hold the draw for the qualification groups in Belfast.

The draw will take place at the International Convention Centre, on Sunday 6th December at 17:00 GMT. Following the announcement in November 2025 that Northern Ireland would host the draw, then-Irish FA president Conrad Kirkwood called it "a proud moment for the Irish FA and for everyone who loves football here in Northern Ireland.".

For the qualification stage of Euro 2028, the 54 teams will be drawn into 12 groups. Groups A-F will have four teams each, whilst Groups G-L have five, with teams playing everyone in their group twice, home and away.

In order to ensure a fair playing field, the groups are drawn from five pots, which are seeded on the interim 2026-27 UEFA Nations League rankings. Pots 1–4 have 12 teams each and Pot 5 has six. The full list of teams in each pot can be found here.

The four co-hosts and Northern Ireland are kept apart in the draw to help boost their chances of qualifying for their home tournament by merit, meaning there will be no home-nation derbies ahead of the tournament.

Nations League quarter-final winners will all go into four-team groups, whilst a five-team group can only include one quarter-final loser or one playoff team, in order to minimize fixture congestion with the Nations League.

After all qualifying games have been held, the 12 group winners and the eight best runners-up will qualify directly, with the remaining four runners-up going into the playoffs.

According to recent reports, for the host nations, qualification will be slightly different from previous tournaments. Instead of qualifying automatically, there is a safety net in place that ensures at least two home nations will qualify. Therefore, if two of England, Scotland, Wales or the Republic of Ireland qualify by merit, then the other two will qualify thanks to the safety net. However, if all four nations fail to qualify, then only the two best ranked nations in the European Qualifiers rankings will be awarded a place at the tournament.

It has been revealed that UEFA streaming service, UEFA TV, will provide coverage of the draw, allowing fans around the world to find out who their nation will face ahead of the tournament in real time. The broadcast will also be shown on UEFA's YouTube channel.

And whilst no UK TV broadcasters have announced that they will show the draw live, UK viewers were able to watch the qualifying draw for the 2026 World Cup on the BBC Sport website and app.

Similarly, viewers in the Republic of Ireland are expected to be able to follow the draw live on RTE Player and the RTE news channel, as with the World Cup draw. However, this is not confirmed just yet.

In a recent development, following the draw on December 6th, the first two qualification games for nations in five-team groups will take place between 26th-30th March 2027, with two more match days between 11th and 15th June. The rest of the groups will then kick off with four games for each team in the elongated international break between 23rd September and 5th October 2027.

According to recent reports, the final two match days will take place during the mid-November international break. Following this, the four group runners-up will enter the playoffs, which will be played out in late-March 2028.

These games will mark the end of the qualification stage, with the final tournament lineup confirmed. All attention will then turn to the National Stadium of Wales in Cardiff, which will host the opening game on the 9th June. Fans can then expect a month of continental tournament mayhem, before Euro 2028 is brought to a close on the 9th July, with the final being held at Wembley Stadium.

#2031. Why malnutrition can go unnoticed, and what that means for our health

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1015 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Why malnutrition can go unnoticed, and what that means for our health

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1015 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some 50,000 deaths can be attributed to malnutrition in Germany each year, according to the German Society for Nutritional Medicine (DGEM).
  • The problem is that malnutrition often doesn't become apparent until the consequences are already severe.
  • "In most cases, you don't notice anything at first," said Matthias Pirlich, a nutritional expert and internal medicine specialist, who once served as DGEM vice president.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some 50,000 deaths can be attributed to malnutrition in Germany each year, according to the German Society for Nutritional Medicine (DGEM).

The problem is that malnutrition often doesn't become apparent until the consequences are already severe.

"In most cases, you don't notice anything at first," said Matthias Pirlich, a nutritional expert and internal medicine specialist, who once served as DGEM vice president. "You could have a severe vitamin D deficiency for months before any symptoms appear at all. The same applies for vitamin B12. By the time symptoms appear, such as nerve damage, it's already too late.".

In a recent development, A long-term B12 deficiency can damage the spinal cord, leading to numbness in the limbs, muscle weakness or even paralysis. Less common deficiency-related brain damage can cause memory loss and mental health challenges.

All B vitamins play an key role in metabolism, blood formation and healthy nerve function.

According to recent reports, vitamins, along with various minerals such as calcium, magnesium, iron, iodine and zinc, are classed as micronutrients. The body needs to source them from food, as it cannot produce them itself. Our bodies also need macronutrients like carbohydrates, carbohydrates, protein and fats that provide us with energy.

According to recent reports, if the body consumes less food than it needs to maintain all bodily functions over a prolonged period of time, then this is known as undernutrition. A recent World Food Organization (FAO) report estimates that approximately 645 million people worldwide suffer from chronic undernutrition.

Malnutrition, on the other hand, occurs when we consume enough calories but lack certain macronutrients or micronutrients in our food. This, too, can make one sick over time and even prove fatal. About 2 billion people worldwide suffer from this so-called hidden hunger, most of them in the Global South. That remarked, even some people in industrialized nations lack important micronutrients in their nutrition.

One study, for instance, found that just under three-quarters of the US population did not meet the recommended daily intake of vitamin D between 2007 and 2010, with more than two-thirds falling short of the recommended amount of vitamin E. And in Germany, about one-third of the population suffered from vitamin D deficiency in 2017, according to the German Nutrition Society. Such deficiency can cause bone, joint and muscle pain. It may also lead to an increased risk of falls and bone fractures.

Sources indicate that about one-third of Germans also had an insufficient intake of iodine, a trace element that is indispensable for the production of thyroid hormones. Iodine deficiency can therefore disrupt normal thyroid function. Not only that — during pregnancy, a baby's brain and nervous system can only properly develop with an adequate supply of iodine.

The cultivation of agricultural produce with partially long shelf life or high yields has in some cases caused a decrease in the micronutrient content of fruits, vegetables and grains. Whether this drop in micronutrients is impacting human health, however, is a matter of debate.

According to recent reports, malnutrition can result from an unbalanced diet that, while filling and providing energy, lacks essential micronutrients. Examples of such empty calories include fast food and highly processed foods, as well as white bread and white rice.

Poverty is often the reason for such an unbalanced diet, for example when people in the Global South can only afford to buy staples such as flour or rice.

Another study found that in Germany, households at risk of poverty are more likely to consume foods that are low in nutrients and high in calories.

It has been revealed that depression is also associated with an increased risk of nutrient deficiency. "People often lose their appetite, and when they neglect their self-care, they may end up eating a very unbalanced diet," Pirlich told DW. His research reveals that older adults and people who live alone often develop malnutrition, too. The risk also increases the more medications a person takes.

Recent findings suggest that many diseases result in the body being less efficient at absorbing or utilizing nutrients through the intestines. This applies to people with inflammatory or chronic disease, such as Crohn's disease, celiac disease, liver disease and cancer.

Recent findings suggest that the DGEM estimates that some 30% of all patients receiving inpatient care in Germany are affected by or at risk of malnutrition. Yet health insurance data indicates that only about 1% of patients are screened and treated for nutrient deficiencies.

Often, patients' malnutrition worsens during their hospital stay. The consequences can be serious, potentially causing additional complications, delayed recuperation, longer hospital stays and even increased mortality rates. This results in higher healthcare expenditure, amounting to billions each year.

Sources indicate that german policymakers and medical associations are therefore developing a proposal to better screen for and treat malnutrition in hospitals. The road map will be ready by 2027 and copy the Dutch approach in the sense that all patients are checked for nutritional deficiencies upon hospital admission.

Pirlich wants to see such screenings for at-risk groups in outpatient clinics, too: "This includes all those with chronic and serious illnesses and, above all, older adults.".

To prevent poverty-related malnutrition, Pirlich suggests increased access to healthy food, offering free school meals as an example.

The nutritional expert recommends eating a diet that is varied and largely plant-based. "Secondary plant compounds have a very positive effect, and if you eat a highly diverse diet, you consume many different foods that are [nutritionally] beneficial," stated Pirlich.

There's a simple rule of thumb: The more colorful your food, the better.

It has been revealed that also, cook vegetables as gently as possible, because overheating and keeping them warm for too long destroys their vitamins. Long storage periods also lead to vitamin loss, so it makes sense to go for seasonal and regional foods in particular.

In a recent development, but even when ensuring a healthy and balanced diet, some people still develop a nutrient deficiency. A blood test can provide clarity, and dietary supplements may help make up for the deficiency.

This article was originally written in German.

Gotham FC, Seattle Reign slam 'atrocious' pitch conditions after NWSL playoff clash

💡 Key Takeaways
  • – Gotham FC head coach Juan Carlos Amoros criticized the field conditions at Sports Illustrated Stadium during the team's 1-0 win over the Seattle Reign on Sunday, a complaint that highlighted the infrastructure battles the league is grappling with during this season's playoffs.
  • According to recent reports, the NWSL fined Gotham $10,000 in the build-up to Sunday's quarterfinal over the quality of the pitch, which appears to have been overworked in recent weeks.
  • It has been revealed that "I feel the obligation to almost apologize for the state of the pitch," Amoros noted post-match.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

HARRISON, N.J. – Gotham FC head coach Juan Carlos Amoros criticized the field conditions at Sports Illustrated Stadium during the team's 1-0 win over the Seattle Reign on Sunday, a complaint that highlighted the infrastructure battles the league is grappling with during this season's playoffs.

According to recent reports, the NWSL fined Gotham $10,000 in the build-up to Sunday's quarterfinal over the quality of the pitch, which appears to have been overworked in recent weeks. Gotham are a secondary tenant at the stadium, which is owned by Upcoming Jersey's Hudson County and is primarily the home of the Red Bull New York. The MLS team played their regular season finale on Saturday evening, less than 24 hours before the 12:30 p.m. local time kickoff for the NWSL match. The stadium also hosted a rugby doubleheader the previous week, the scars of which were easy to spot over the course of Sunday's game.

It has been revealed that "I feel the obligation to almost apologize for the state of the pitch," Amoros noted post-match. "I think at this level, in this kind of game, as a league, we should be having a better surface. Unfortunately, our football club did absolutely everything in their power to make sure that was the case. Unfortunately, it wasn't but luckily, it looks like nobody got hurt and the game was what it was.".

Players on both teams complained of the playing conditions, including Gotham's Jaelin Howell, who worked her way back from an ankle issue in time for Sunday's match.

"Obviously it's pretty sandy out there and so a little unstable but I want to be able to give my all to the team and everything I got and so obviously can't think about that," Howell said. "The other team has to play on that, too, so we acknowledged it and we moved on and I think that our team managed it pretty well for the most part.".

The Reign's Jess Fishlock, a member of Seattle's squad since the inaugural NWSL season in 2013 who played the final match of her career, was more harsh in her assessment of the field.

"We performed so well for this group of players to come against a team like that at home on this field, which is atrocious, just saying it out loud," she said.

Her comments were echoed by Reign coach Laura Harvey, who has worked in and around the league since its inception.

Recent findings suggest that "Let's be real, there's no way a playoff game should be played on that shit," she told ESPN post-match. "I just can't believe they've allowed it. They knew it last week.".

Amoros mentioned the field conditions ultimately impacted Gotham's ability to perform on Sunday, the NWSL Shield winners stringing together a performance he described as "not the best football match that you will ever see.".

Sources indicate that "When you play on a pitch like that, you cannot be thinking of the next action or what you're gonna do once you get that ball," he said. "You need to be looking at the ball because he can bounce at any given time. Plus, it just changes the whole dynamic of the game and it changes the dynamic of how we play. We adapted certain things. We adapted certain things on the game strategy. We had to be a bit more direct and certain situations but it definitely affected the way we played, yes.".

Recent findings suggest that gotham will conclude play at Sports Illustrated Stadium next Sunday at 3 p.m. local time in the NWSL semifinals against the Kansas City Current. The Red Bulls, who missed the MLS Cup playoffs for a second consecutive season, will host another match the night before, this time a friendly against Club America during the men's international break.

The pitch was an understandable obstacle for both teams but Gotham's struggles did not end there. The reigning champions, who are favored to win the championship for the third time in four seasons after winning the Shield, were second-best against the lowest-seeded team in the postseason. They benefitted from a fourth minute own goal from Jordyn Bugg, forced by standout Jaedyn Shaw, but were unable to actually assert any sort of dominance as the game progressed.

An unfortunate own goal and Gotham take the early lead ‼️NWSL Playoffs presented by Google Pixel pic.twitter.com/4LwZdfgLpx.

In a recent development, gotham did not take a single shot on target over the course of the game, their six shots totaling just 0.17 expected goals. The Reign were not all that much better but momentum shifted their way in the second half, eventually racking up 11 shots and 0.54 expected goals. The visitors were stymied by Gotham defenders Tierna Davidson and Jess Carter, as well as 2024 goalkeeper of the year Ann-Katrin Berger.

Industry observers note that "She literally does it on a consistent basis," Shaw noted about Berger. "It's crazy the kind of saves that she makes and I feel like she makes a worldly save at least once a game and I mean I think it's hard enough getting through a back line but to get through Ann is a whole other task and I think we're all really grateful to have her back there. I know I am as an attacker and I think we all just have full trust in her ability and she's just such an integral part of our team and the way that we like to play as well. Even from the goal, she's such a substantial piece of the way that we play and our style.".

AKB goes aerial to deny Mia Fishel a goal ✈️ pic.twitter.com/4lqMm623On.

Gotham's attack, though, had no such excuses. Midfielder Rose Lavelle exited the match at halftime as the coaching staff manages her minutes after dealing with a knock in recent weeks, her exit diluting their attack. Forward Sam Kerr, meanwhile, failed to register a single shot and took just 23 touches over the course of 90 minutes in an absent performance during an inconsistent return to the NWSL. The Australia international has scored just four goals in 18 games since joining Gotham in July, despite the fact that she has racked up 9.67 expected goals along the way.

Amoros credited the Reign for their ability to lock out Gotham's defense.

In a recent development, "I think they did a good job trying to stop certain situations," he said. "I think that was the key. They did really well on the press. They were first and second in a lot of the duels and they obviously play short passes to then go diagonal, which obviously then is something difficult to defend and something that is a lot more doable than probably over a style of play. It's just different and we had complications with those situations to defend. At the same time, we defended them. I think that's the key.".

Shaw, who attempted to spearhead a lifeless Gotham attack, described a disjointed performance that the team will hope not to replicate the following week.

Industry observers note that "I think we just need to be cleaner on the ball," Shaw noted. "Obviously, the surface doesn't really help but  just in general, I think we can be more comfortable on the ball, facing forward and just be clinical in our passes, which I think will help us get to the final third a little bit more with more quality chances on goal.".

Although Arsenal have been linked with Endrick by TEAMtalk and others, it now looks like Serie A might be a more realistic option for the 20-year-old.

Endrick looked like the real deal when he first burst onto the scene as a teenager at former club Palmeiras, but it just hasn’t happened for him at Real Madrid.

It could still be that Endrick will have a fine career at the highest level, but he surely needs to find a new club soon, even if it’s claimed that Mourinho wants him as part of his squad.

Endrick shone during a loan spell at Lyon last season, so a similar spell with someone like Milan could be ideal for him in the near future.

Arsenal could also surely find a role for the youngster as they need a bit more in attack, but it’s perhaps also far from guaranteed that he’d be a regular starter in Mikel Arteta’s side.

Want more CaughtOffside coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

The Gunners already have Kai Havertz and Viktor Gyokeres as their main striker options, and even if they could do with an upgrade, it doesn’t look like Endrick would necessarily find it easy to get into the team ahead of those two on a regular basis.

Will Australia push for fossil fuel exit at UN talks?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In its role as president of negotiations at the UN climate talks in Turkey, Australia is being pressured to guide nations toward unified action on slashing the greenhouse gas emissions that are generated in large part by burning fossil fuels.
  • The nation has pledged to lead by example at the summit through a strong commitment to renewable energy, electrification and reduced reliance on planet-heating coal, oil and gas.
  • "Renewable energy, grids, storage and electrification are creating opportunities to strengthen resilience, improve energy security, and reduce emissions at the same time," said Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister, in October during a meeting in Fiji ahead of the COP climate conference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In its role as president of negotiations at the UN climate talks in Turkey, Australia is being pressured to guide nations toward unified action on slashing the greenhouse gas emissions that are generated in large part by burning fossil fuels.

The nation has pledged to lead by example at the summit through a strong commitment to renewable energy, electrification and reduced reliance on planet-heating coal, oil and gas.

"Renewable energy, grids, storage and electrification are creating opportunities to strengthen resilience, improve energy security, and reduce emissions at the same time," said Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister, in October during a meeting in Fiji ahead of the COP climate conference.

It has been revealed that "These are proven, commercial and scalable today. Now is the moment for faster implementation.".

Yet Australia is also the world's third-largest exporter of fossil fuels. And unlike France and Germany, or island nations from Fiji to the Bahamas that are highly vulnerable to a changing climate, the COP31 co-president has not yet committed to phasing them out.

As calls grow for the country to set a clear route to a clean energy future, critics say its vague promise to transition away from polluting sources of power does not go far enough.

Australia is home to 56% of the world's coal mine projects currently in the pipeline, notes environmental nonprofit, 350.org.

Andreas Sieber, head of political strategy at the organization, is calling on the country, the world's second-largest coal exporter, to reverse course and announce an "overdue coal phaseout date" during the COP31 conference.

"Australia needs to walk the walk and follow Germany's example and commit to a phaseout," said Melanie Pill, founder of The Climate Project, an Australia-based climate policy advisory.

The argument to end fossil fuel production is not only about cutting emissions but reducing dependence on energy systems that rely on volatile oil and gas markets, she explained.

"A fossil phaseout in the face of the enduring and escalating conflict in the Middle East is in the interest of everyone," Pill told DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

This is especially true for Australia's diesel-reliant Pacific neighbors, who spend up to 25% of GDP on fossil fuel imports — as opposed 6% on health — according to a report by the Institute for Climate Risk and Response at the University of New South Wales.

As lead negotiator at the UN climate talks, Australia can "flip the narrative" on a fossil fuel phaseout, using the challenge of energy security as a justification, said Pill.

This opportunity could be lost, however, if Australia fails to address fossil fuel exports that accounted for 80% of its total carbon footprint in 2022 — and near 5% of global emissions.

While the nation is a world leader in rooftop solar, and generates around half of its electricity from renewables, this progress is "being undone by its continued approval of more fossil fuels for export," stated Simon Bradshaw, COP31 lead and climate expert at Greenpeace Australia Pacific.

He noted that the Labor government of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has approved the construction, expansion or extension of 38 coal, oil and gas projects since coming to power four years ago on a pro-climate platform.

"You cannot aspire to lead on climate abroad if you're not getting your own house in order," noted Thomas Houlie, climate and energy policy analyst at Climate Analytics, a global climate policy institute.

In 2025, when Australia approved the extension of a major gas export project in the country's west until 2070, Albanese justified the move in the name of a balance between "security of energy supply" and "support [for] the transition which reduces our emissions.".

It has been revealed that the country has publicly backed a global transition away from the fossil fuels driving the global temperature rise linked to extreme heat and drought. Both through the Global Stocktake agreed at the 2023 UN climate summit, and via the inaugural "transitioning away" summit in Colombia this April, at which Australia and 56 countries pledged to develop a fossil fuel exit road map.

But these commitments are not reflected in Australian resources policy, or its domestic rollout of clean power infrastructure.

"While the government has set a renewables target for electricity, it leaves plenty of blind spots in other sectors," said Houlie, adding that emission reductions in industry and transport have been limited and that the push to achieve an 82% renewables target for the electricity grid by 2030 is behind schedule.

In its role as lead negotiator at COP31, Australia has promised to ensure that any final conference text serves to "elevate the views and the experiences" of small Pacific nations in its region, from Vanuatu to Tuvalu.

These island countries that generate low emissions yet suffer extreme climate impacts from worsening cyclones or rising seas are "sick of Australia's double talk on climate," noted Shiva Gounden, head of Pacific at Greenpeace Australia Pacific.

Recent findings suggest that australia must commit to "substantial new funding contributions" to help Pacific neighbors adapt to the climate emergency and achieve energy independence, said his colleague Bradshaw. He reiterated the need to concurrently create a "national road map" away from coal and gas production and export.

A Climate Analytics report co-authored by Houlie outlines a fossil fuel phaseout pathway for Australia that can begin immediately. This includes an end to coal power generation by 2034 and a rapid reduction in oil and gas consumption, with renewables generating almost all the country's electricity by 2040. Fossil fuel export projects would be eliminated, and existing ones shuttered before becoming obsolete.

"This co-presidency is a golden opportunity for Australia to step up and commit to a phaseout," remarked Houlie.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

So where do Manchester United go from here? It is never a good look when opposition fans start willing a rival club to stick with their manager, but that was the ignominy that had befallen Michael Carrick by the end of an afternoon in which Lisandro Martinez’s latest plastic hardman impression embodied the very worst of United’s self-sabotage.

After seeing their team go 2-0 up when Cole Palmer converted the penalty given away by Martinez’s lunacy, the Chelsea fans taunted Carrick with chants of “You’re getting sacked in the morning” and later “You’re going down with the City”, a nod to the other Manchester club who are crisis torn for very different reasons.

As the final whistle loomed, though, and with United just grateful Estevao had not punished Martinez’s red card more severely, the Chelsea fans had changed their tune. “Michael Carrick, we want you to stay,” came the chant from the Matthew Harding Stand and that cut far deeper.

And to think that the opening 45 minutes had offered United and their fans some hope of a little respite from the storm before ultimately giving way to an ever-darkening gloom.

Industry observers note that carrick, who had been given a stay of execution in midweek, said he still expected to be in charge for Roma’s visit to Old Trafford on Tuesday in the Champions League. But it is hard to escape the feeling that another managerial change will be coming at United before too long even if no one can be sure what happens next.

Equally, the prospect of more upheaval in the dugout might elicit little more than a shrug from fans pointing the finger squarely at the ownership and the executives they have appointed. The players were spared this time but Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazers remained the target of sustained abuse as did Jason Wilcox, the director of football.

Recent findings suggest that defeat here extended United’s winless run to nine matches, their worst sequence for 38 years. They have taken just four points from the last 21 on offer in the Premier League and seem to be sinking fast. Carrick was asked about the team becoming mired in a relegation battle. This is the territory United are in.

The strange thing is this could and probably should have been a day when they at least stopped the rot for a few days. But more non-existent defending and brainlessness from Martinez, who was sent off for planting an elbow in Wesley Fofana’s face, put paid to that in a second half in which Carrick admitted United “unravelled”.

According to recent reports, chelsea were cut open on at least five occasions in a see-saw first half and Matheus Cunha also had a goal disallowed for a narrow offside. Xabi Alonso’s side had opportunities of their own – you will always get them against this United team – but they were second best and lucky not to be behind. Everyone talks about United being there for the taking, but the truth is Chelsea, coming off the back of a miserable defeat to Spurs and Carabao Cup exit to Liverpool, were here.

It has been revealed that the problem is Carrick’s team could not hit a barn door at the moment. They have scored just three goals in their last six league games and that lack of cutting edge was evident in the way Bruno Fernandes, back in the team as captain, and Amad Diallo (dangerous but with no end product) wasted excellent chances. That wastefulness would put pressure on any back line, let alone one with all the fortitude of wet cardboard. Chelsea were spared and exploited it with the help of the second and most corrosive acts of United’s self-mutilation.

We will come to Martinez’s sending off in a moment, but there had already been a cowardly act of a different kind from the Argentine defender before then in the lead-up to Chelsea’s opening goal soon after the restart.
